KEY MESSAGE 1 DESCRIPTION...

A nor'easter centered 185 miles east of DelMarVa will drift NNE 
towards 40N/70W benchmark through this evening. Models are in 
agreement that the center of the system will make a decision turn 
westward towards Long Island and New Jersey tonight into Sunday. The 
nor'easter will become vertically stacked and start to fill Sunday 
night and will slowly move across southern New England through 
Tuesday.

The main take away from recent observations and forecast trends has 
been a decrease in storm surge. This is primarily a result of 
the southward trend in the storm track. Storm surge models have 
trended down and have incorporated this into the latest forecast
with surge holding around 1.0 ft, peaking below 1.5 ft. While 
total water level forecasts come up just short of minor flood 
stage, have left the Coastal Flood Advisory unchanged. Large 
near shore waves will bring ample splash over that will bring 
debris onto vulnerable coastal roadways through at least the 
next three high tide cycles. In addition, dune erosion is 
expected and the most vulnerable locations will see the 
potential for some inundation.

Hazardous conditions at the beaches and over the waters are observed 
and are expected to continue through at least Sunday night. Latest 
observations show near shore waves pushing 9 feet with an 11 second 
period with waves offshore near Jeffrey's Ledge at 14 feet with an 
11 second period. Waves are expected to increase into this evening 
and then hold steady through Sunday before subsiding Sunday night. 
The High Surf Advisory that runs through Sunday remains unchanged to 
cover the hazardous conditions from large waves and strong rip 
currents. It is important to note that the long duration of a long 
fetch will create opportunities for sneaker waves that will be 
larger embedded waves in a set and have potential to run farther 
into shore. Therefore, extra caution is encouraged for those 
venturing to the beach to observed the surf and avoid rock outcrops 
and jetties. 

KEY MESSAGE 2 DESCRIPTION...

The well advertised nor'easter will continue to drift north for
a little bit longer before stalling out somewhere off the coast
of New Jersey by early Sunday. We have seen a couple bands of
light rain move into the area, gradually moistening the
atmosphere from south to north. Gusty winds and precipitation
chances will be on the increase through the rest of the day 
with periods of moderate to heavy rain possible through Monday.
Areas south of the mountains and along the coast should see a
widespread 1 to 2 inches of rain while the latest HREF guidance
suggests a potential for higher amounts over far southeast New
Hampshire and far southwest Maine. Here, localized totals up to
4 inches will be possible through Monday. CAMs suggest that
precipitation will likely come in waves with a convective
component. Therefore, a stray bolt of lightning may not be
impossible along the coast and over the waters. Embedded
downpours will also be possible with P-wats in the 90th
percentile or greater for this time of year. While most of the
precipitation will start to taper off later in the day on
Monday, the upper low will move overhead on Tuesday which may
lead to some lingering areas of light rain. 

Our area will be under a decent pressure gradient with high pressure 
to the north and the nor'easter to our south but the threat for 
stronger winds may have backed off just a bit as the low continues 
to trend further south. Forecast soundings at Portsmouth still 
suggest we could see some winds in the 40 to 45 knot range at the 
top of the mixed layer across southeast New Hampshire late Saturday 
through Sunday morning but available momentum should decreasing 
north and east. In general, it appears that the strongest gusts will 
be over portions of southeastern New Hampshire and southwest Maine 
to around 40 mph. Elsewhere expect breezy northeast winds gusting 25 
to 35 mph. While winds will not be overly strong, this will be a 
rather long duration event. We will likely see the strongest
gusts later today through Sunday morning, but breezy conditions
will last into at least Monday. Thus, with plenty of leaves on 
the trees there could be a limited power outage threat, 
especially along the coast and portions of the interior.

KEY MESSAGE 3 DESCRIPTION...

After the nor'easter moves offshore, the 500mb pattern looks to
favor the development of a ridge over the eastern US. In 
addition to high pressure moving in south of the northeast, this
could allow for above average temperatures in the second half 
of next week. High pressure, while not exactly onto of the 
region, should keep most places dry. Some very weak instability 
could allow for a stray shower to generate on Wednesday or 
Thursday, but most people should stay dry.
